case_study_insert.main_stem: Meadowlands Poultry (MPP) is a sole trader business in the poultry farming and meat processing sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2007 by farmer Aisha Meadowlands, it supplies packaged chicken to regional supermarkets and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. MPP plans to invest $880,000 in a new automated poultry processing and packaging line, financed by a $480,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 from the sale of unused farmland. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. MPP faces two problems: a 3.1% defect rate on the packaging line and rising labour turnover.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q4 2025: The packaging line processed 21,000 birds last quarter at a defect rate of 3.1%, down from 4.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 29 per month. Average delivery time to regional supermarkets is 2.9 days. Carcass waste measured 3.7% of output. Labour turnover reached 12% over the year, but a pilot bonus scheme reduced absence on the packaging shift. A survey of 650 supermarket shoppers found 69% would pay up to $0.70 more for free-range packaged chicken and 60% check animal-welfare labels. Training logs show 14 of 30 staff need on-the-job training on the new packer; off-the-job training at the agriculture college costs $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Meadowlands Poultry as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.10% to 4.85%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.05 to $13.95 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Feed grain and packaging input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 6.6%, while consumer spending on free-range chicken grew 4.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: MPP plans to fund part of its packaging line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MPP of using the sale of unused farmland instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling unused farmland raises $400,000 in cash without any interest payments or capital repayments, unlike the $480,000 bank loan, so MPP's cash flow is protected while it already carries fixed costs of $280,000 a year. The proceeds can go directly into the $880,000 packaging line and help absorb the 9.8% rise in feed grain and packaging costs without raising the $13.00 selling price charged to regional supermarkets.

Point 2: Asset sale finance needs no collateral on the trading business and carries no repossession risk, so the new processing line cannot be seized if demand for packaged chicken falls. It also keeps control firmly with Aisha Meadowlands as sole trader, since no lender can impose conditions on how the farm is run. Because the land was unused, the sale releases idle value rather than taking on new debt, and it avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base rate rose from 4.10% to 4.85%. Overall, the sale is cheaper and less risky than borrowing more.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MPP and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: MPP is launching its new free-range packaged chicken range. Consider a television advertising campaign, sponsorship of a local sports club, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MPP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising campaign: Television would give the free-range chicken range wide reach quickly across many regions. However, airtime and production costs are high for a 30-employee sole trader already funding an $880,000 line with a $480,000 loan, and much of the mass audience will not shop at the regional supermarkets that stock MPP, so a large part of the spend would be wasted.

Sponsorship of a local sports club: Sponsorship can build goodwill and community ties that fit the 60% of surveyed shoppers who check animal-welfare labels, and it is cheaper than television. Its reach is narrow and the link to free-range chicken is indirect, so it may do little to shift product off supermarket shelves in the short term.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can explain free-range and welfare benefits to a targeted audience at low cost per reached shopper and speak directly to the 69% of 650 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.70 more. Results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility, but the message supports the premium positioning.

Recommendation: MPP should choose social media influencer marketing as the lead channel, with a small local sponsorship to build community goodwill. Influencers reach the exact welfare-conscious segment in the research, cost far less than television, and can justify the $0.70 premium. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a sole trader servicing a $480,000 loan, and sponsorship is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is narrow and its connection to packaged chicken is weaker than a targeted welfare message.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MPP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MPP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: MPP's labour turnover has risen and defect rates are high. Explain two benefits for MPP of using a bonus scheme to motivate its packaging team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus scheme links extra pay to meeting quality and output targets, giving the 30 employees a financial incentive to reduce the 3.1% defect rate and the 12% labour turnover reported in the operations log. The pilot bonus scheme already reduced absence on the packaging shift, showing that rewards can improve attendance and keep skilled staff, which is vital under autocratic leadership where Aisha Meadowlands sets strict standards.

Point 2: Bonuses can be tied to cutting the 3.7% carcass waste, so workers gain directly from less waste and the $7.00 contribution per unit is protected. Keeping experienced operators also lowers the $850 per employee off-the-job training cost caused by frequent turnover and protects output of 95,000 units while the new $880,000 packaging line beds in. A bonus is paid only when performance improves, so it is self-funding compared with a fixed wage rise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MPP's turnover, defects and output.

questions.question_text: MPP must upskill 14 packaging staff to operate the new packer. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the agriculture college. Which should MPP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training 14 staff on MPP's own packer is directly relevant to the firm's exact settings and hygiene standards, costs nothing in external fees, and keeps those workers productive while they learn, protecting output toward 95,000 units and the drive to cut the 3.1% defect rate. The drawback is that trainers are themselves production staff whose work suffers, and bad habits can be passed on, which matters while carcass waste is 3.7%.

Off-the-job training: The agriculture college course at $850 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 14 staff, costing $11,900 in total — small beside the $880,000 line. It removes 14 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity and risking more defects, and the generic content may not match MPP's exact packer, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: MPP should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short college modules later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while the defect rate is 3.1% and labour turnover is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $11,900 and 14 staff from a new line would jeopardise supply to regional supermarkets, and MPP can add certification once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MPP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of MPP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MPP with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MPP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $6.00) = $280,000 ÷ $7.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.00 − $6.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MPP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. MPP's managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 95,000 units to confirm the packaging line is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 55,000 units, which supports running the new $880,000 line near capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.00 lets MPP model the $0.70 free-range premium: if won, contribution rises toward $7.70, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $280,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $280,000 and contribution of $7.00 lets managers set the sales volume needed to service the $480,000 bank loan and check the line can afford repayments before committing more capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost ($280,000 ÷ 95,000 units + $6.00 = $8.95 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, isolate the 3.7% carcass waste, and judge whether to renegotiate the $6.00 variable cost given 9.8% feed inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 95,000-unit output; the $0.70 free-range premium against $280,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $480,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.95 to tackle 3.7% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MPP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MPP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.61 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $245,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $120,000 + $75,000 = $290,000. Liquidity cover for 2024 = $245,000 ÷ $175,000 = 1.40, and for 2025 = $290,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.61. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($245,000 − $110,000) ÷ $175,000 = $135,000 ÷ $175,000 = 0.77, and 2025 = ($290,000 − $95,000) ÷ $180,000 = $195,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: MPP's short-term liquidity has strengthened. The first ratio rose from 1.40 to 1.61 as current assets grew from $245,000 to $290,000 while current liabilities rose only from $175,000 to $180,000, so the business covers its short-term debts more comfortably. The second ratio, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.77 to 1.08, so MPP is no longer dependent on selling chicken stock to meet obligations — useful while it services a $480,000 bank loan and builds an $880,000 packaging line. However, trade receivables rose from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up cash; if regional supermarkets pay late the position could weaken, and the fall in inventories to $95,000 should be watched to avoid shortages.

Conclusion: MPP's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.40 to 1.61 and 0.77 to 1.08), and the improvement does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so MPP should tighten credit control with its supermarket customers while proceeding with the packaging investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether MPP's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MPP of positioning its packaged chicken as free-range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free-range positioning matches the 69% of 650 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.70 more for free-range packaged chicken, letting MPP charge a premium that protects the $7.00 contribution per unit even as feed grain and packaging costs rise 9.8%. It also appeals to the 60% who check animal-welfare labels, helping keep listings with regional supermarkets for the $880,000 line.

Disadvantage: Free-range production usually costs more per bird than intensive farming, keeping the $6.00 variable cost per unit high and squeezing margins unless the $0.70 premium is accepted. A higher defect rate could also undo the gain: the 3.1% defect rate and 3.7% carcass waste already pressure output, and any welfare-related supply shortfall would make the premium difficult to deliver consistently.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MPP's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.85%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect MPP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.10% to 4.85%): If MPP's $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $480,000 = $3,600 a year (0.0075 × $480,000). That is modest against $280,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $880,000 line, but MPP can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $13.95 an hour): MPP employs a workforce of 30 in processing and packing, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 95,000 units ÷ 30 staff = 3,166.67 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $7.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.8% feed grain and packaging): MPP's $6.00 variable cost per unit contains feed and packaging, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% that adds about 9.8% × $6.00 = $0.59 per unit, and at 95,000 units that is roughly $56,000 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.70 free-range premium and supermarket price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 95,000 units and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that justifies the $880,000 line, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $3,600, so both are smaller.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MPP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MPP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MPP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
